course.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine
course.institution: Stanford University, Computer Science Department (paper, WWW7 conference, 1998)
course.level: research paper; the PageRank part needs only fractions and percentages

units.title: Introduction
units.summary: Argues that web search in the late 1990s returned too many low-quality keyword matches, that hand-built directories could not keep up with the web's growth, and sets the goals of high-precision results and an open academic platform for large-scale search research.
key_ideas: search as an academic research platform

units.title: System Features: PageRank and Anchor Text
units.summary: Introduces PageRank, a citation-style importance score where a link counts more if it comes from an important page with few outgoing links, computed iteratively and explained as the long-run share of time a randomly clicking surfer, who occasionally jumps to a random page, spends on each page; also uses link anchor text as a description of the target page and records word positions and font details.

units.title: Related Work
units.summary: Places the system against earlier web crawlers and search engines and classical information retrieval, explaining why techniques tuned on small, homogeneous, curated collections break down on the heterogeneous, uncontrolled and adversarial web.

units.title: System Anatomy
units.summary: Describes the architecture end to end: distributed crawlers feed a compressed repository, an indexer turns pages into hit lists stored in barrels as a forward index, a sorter builds the inverted index, and the searcher combines type-weighted hit counts, word proximity and PageRank into a final ranking.
key_ideas: ranking from hit types, proximity and PageRank

units.title: Results and Performance
units.summary: Reports a sample query result list, the storage needed for roughly 24 million pages, crawl and indexing throughput, and query response times, arguing the design is already practical at that scale.

units.title: Conclusions and Future Work
units.summary: Summarizes the contributions (link-based quality ranking, anchor text, proximity) and lists future directions such as smarter crawl scheduling, query caching, user feedback, personalized ranking and making the system a shared research tool.

units.title: Advertising and Mixed Motives
units.summary: Argues that advertising-funded search engines have incentives that conflict with users' interest in the best results, and that a transparent academic search engine is therefore valuable.

units.title: Scalability
units.summary: Argues the system can grow to about 100 million pages before operating-system limits bite, and that centralized text indexing will keep getting cheaper with hardware doublings, while distributed indexing is elegant but costly to administer.
